items.title: Rabbit’s New Cloud OS Leverages Your Laptop for Enhanced Performance
items.summary: A Santa Monica-based company known for its r1 handheld device has launched OS3, an agentic operating system designed to execute user-defined tasks through cloud-based processing. Overview of OS3 The system operates by deploying a local agent on connected devices, which communicates with Rabbit’s cloud infrastructure to perform actions. Users interact with the platform via a chat interface, specifying objectives that the OS3 agent then fulfills by leveraging desktop applications, local files, web resources, or code execution across multiple devices. Device Integration and Agent Functionality The agent can link up to five devices, including Windows, Mac, and Linux computers, cloud virtual machines, dedicated AI hardware, and the r1. Once installed, the agent grants Rabbit’s servers direct access to the machine’s resources, enabling the system to process user requests. Data Handling and Privacy Claims The company asserts that the local agent does not copy, store, retain, or monetize user files, which remain on the host device. Instead, conversation history and contextual memory generated during interactions are stored on Rabbit’s servers. When a task is executed, Rabbit’s servers analyze the relevant data and prompts before forwarding them to the user’s chosen AI model provider. Security and User Control Rabbit emphasizes that OS3 requires explicit user approval for sensitive operations. The host operating system must request system-level permissions locally, and users can revoke access at any time. However, the company has not specified which actions qualify as sensitive. Customization and Skills The platform supports “skills”—packaged instructions or tools that expand the agent’s capabilities. Users can integrate these skills by pasting a URL into the chat interface, allowing OS3 to configure them without requiring command-line input or additional configuration files. This streamlined process, however, bypasses opportunities for users to review the code or functionality they are granting access to. AI Model Integration and Flexibility Users can customize the system by supplying API keys from third-party AI providers, cloud platforms, or locally hosted models. Switching between models does not disrupt existing context, memory, or skill configurations. CEO’s Vision and Availability Rabbit’s founder and CEO, Jesse Lyu, described OS3 as a system that eliminates the need for direct user interaction, instead focusing on delivering desired outcomes. OS3 is currently available at os3.rabbit.tech, following 12 months of iterative updates to Rabbit’s existing software ecosystem. Implications and Concerns This platform represents a shift toward agentic AI systems, where software autonomously executes tasks based on high-level user instructions. However, its reliance on cloud infrastructure and third-party model providers raises questions about data handling, transparency, and security controls. Recent developments in cybersecurity highlight growing concerns around such technologies, including malware leveraging AI for dynamic decision-making, domain hijacking campaigns, and deepfake-related risks. Enterprises adopting agentic systems must carefully evaluate their trust models and data governance practices.

items.title: Nagaland Cybercrime: 85% of Reported Cases From Two Cities
items.summary: Dimapur and Kohima account for approximately 80% to 85% of all cybercrime reports in Nagaland, according to the Cyber Crime Police Station at Police Headquarters. Primary Sources of Cybercrime Dimapur and Kohima serve as the primary sources of incidents involving deceptive practices, financial exploitation, and unauthorized access to personal information. The most frequently documented offenses include fraudulent activities, identity impersonation, and monetary scams, which often involve perpetrators posing as legitimate entities to manipulate victims into disclosing sensitive data or transferring funds. Common Cybercrime Tactics The majority of reported cybercrimes in the region involve tactics such as phishing, smishing, and vishing. Phishing attacks typically rely on deceptive digital communications, such as emails or messages, to coerce individuals into revealing confidential details or engaging in risky actions. Smishing leverages text messages to achieve similar outcomes, while vishing employs voice calls to build trust and extract information. These methods highlight the importance of scrutinizing unsolicited communications, particularly those requesting financial transactions or personal data. Investment Fraud and Scams Investment fraud has emerged as a significant threat, with scammers utilizing social media platforms to promote unrealistic return-on-investment opportunities. These advertisements often exploit users’ desire for rapid financial gains, leading to substantial losses. Cybercriminals frequently employ persuasive language and fabricated testimonials to enhance the credibility of their schemes. Red Flags and Recommendations Users are advised to remain vigilant against unsolicited messages, calls, or online content that request money or sensitive information. Red flags include unexpected requests for immediate action, promises of unusually high returns, and links or attachments from unknown sources. Individuals who suspect they are targeted should refrain from making additional payments or sharing further details with the perpetrator. Preserving evidence such as messages, call logs, and transaction records is critical for reporting incidents to authorities. Human Error and Cybersecurity Awareness The prevalence of these crimes underscores the role of human error in cyber threats. Cybercriminals often initiate attacks through simple interactions, such as a deceptive message or a convincing phone call, rather than relying on advanced technical exploits. Users are encouraged to verify unexpected requests through independent channels, avoid sharing banking or personal information without confirmation, and exercise caution when engaging with online advertisements promising exceptional financial benefits.

items.title: Gas Bill Scam or Trap? Fake APK App Targets Consumers
items.summary: Law enforcement agencies have launched a public awareness initiative to combat a growing cyber fraud scheme targeting consumers of a specific gas service provider. Public Awareness Initiative The operation involves collaboration with local housing associations and the distribution of alerts through multiple channels to educate residents on identifying and avoiding deceptive tactics. Police Investigation Findings The police investigation into reported incidents has revealed that cybercriminals are exploiting personal data linked to the gas service to target individuals. Fraudulent Activities and Preventive Measures Similar fraudulent activities have been documented in other regions, prompting authorities to implement preventive measures. Officials emphasized that possession of a consumer’s name, address, or service details does not validate the authenticity of a caller or message. Deceptive Communications Consumers are being misled through unsolicited communications, including text messages, phone calls, and digital platforms, which claim that their gas meter or billing information requires immediate attention. These messages often threaten disconnection unless a specific action is taken. Malicious APK Files Fraudsters distribute malicious Android Package Kit (APK) files, disguised as official updates, such as “Meter Update.apk” or “Green Gas Meter Update.” Installing these files grants attackers remote access to devices, enabling them to steal sensitive data and siphon funds from financial accounts. Financial Laundering and Reporting Investigations have uncovered methods used to launder illicit proceeds. Funds obtained through the scam are allegedly redirected to settle utility bills, with victims sometimes enticed by offers of discounts or financial incentives to facilitate transactions. Authorities are examining these financial flows as part of their broader probe into the distribution of stolen assets. Consumer Advice Residents are advised to verify any claims of service disruptions through official customer support channels, the verified mobile application, or direct contact with the service provider. Users must avoid engaging with unsolicited links, downloading APKs from unknown sources, or sharing confidential information such as One-Time Passwords (OTPs), card details, or banking credentials. Reporting Incidents Victims of cyber fraud are urged to report incidents immediately via the 1930 helpline. Prompt reporting allows authorities to initiate investigations and secure relevant digital evidence. Detailed procedures for filing online complaints are available to guide affected individuals through the process. Scam Tactics and Red Flags The scam exploits psychological pressure by creating a sense of urgency, compelling users to act without verifying the legitimacy of requests. Experts warn that unexpected threats of service termination, unsolicited APK installations, or demands for financial information are red flags requiring immediate scrutiny. Verification through official communication channels is critical to preventing further exploitation. “Authorities emphasized that possession of a consumer’s name, address, or service details does not validate the authenticity of a caller or message.” “Experts warn that unexpected threats of service termination, unsolicited APK installations, or demands for financial information are red flags requiring immediate scrutiny.”

items.title: How Organized Crime Syndicates Use Gift Card Fraud for Cross-Border Money Laundering
items.summary: International law enforcement investigations have uncovered a growing trend of transnational criminal organizations leveraging gift card fraud to facilitate cross-border money laundering. Criminal Networks Exploit Gift Card Fraud as a Tool for International Money Laundering These groups systematically convert illicit proceeds from schemes such as romance scams, elder exploitation, cyberattacks, and physical theft into retail gift cards. By bypassing traditional banking systems, they use digital card balances to acquire high-value electronics and arrange international shipments, creating complex financial trails that hinder investigative efforts. Layered Transactions Obscure Illicit Money Trails A federal indictment of a Chinese national revealed a large-scale operation accused of channeling fraud-generated funds through gift card transactions. The scheme involved converting card balances into electronics shipped directly to China, according to law enforcement documents. Physical Store Racks and Fraudulent Portals Targeted Criminal networks employ diverse tactics to siphon value from retail distribution systems. One method involves tampering with physical store displays, where perpetrators extract serial numbers and PINs from visible gift cards before repackaging them to avoid detection. When unsuspecting customers purchase and activate these cards, fraudsters monitor the transactions to drain the balances. Simultaneously, syndicates operate counterfeit websites designed to mimic legitimate brand portals. Users who enter card credentials on these phishing platforms inadvertently transfer control of the funds to criminals. Stolen balances are either immediately converted into retail purchases or traded through underground networks. A major gaming company recently suspended physical gift card sales due to escalating security risks linked to these activities. Expansion into Digital Coupons and Consumer Risks The scope of fraud has expanded beyond traditional gift cards to include digital coupons and alternative payment instruments. Authorities in Georgia recently arrested individuals involved in manufacturing counterfeit digital vouchers, highlighting the diversification of criminal techniques. In India, where digital vouchers are increasingly used for gaming, streaming, and e-commerce, consumers face heightened risks. Fraudsters exploit this trend through deceptive tactics such as fake job offers, investment scams, lottery claims, and staged legal threats. Cybersecurity Advisories for Consumers Cybersecurity advisories recommend that individuals refuse gift card purchase requests from unknown sources, inspect product packaging for tampering, access balance verification tools exclusively through official apps, and report suspicious activity to cybercrime authorities. The evolving nature of gift card-based fraud underscores the need for enhanced security measures and public awareness to mitigate financial losses and protect vulnerable populations.

items.title: NetBSD 10.2 security fixes close a remote kernel bug in ipfilter
items.summary: A NetBSD box at the edge of a network, filtering traffic with ipfilter, has been carrying a kernel flaw that someone outside the machine can set off. The bug is a remotely triggerable null pointer dereference in ipfilter, meaning the kernel tries to read memory through a pointer that leads nowhere. In kernel code, that usually ends with the whole system going down. The NetBSD Project shipped the fix on September 15 in NetBSD 10.2, … More →

items.title: A Vulnerability in F5 BIG-IP Access Policy Manager Could Allow for Remote Code Execution
items.summary: A vulnerability has been discovered in F5 BIG-IP Access Policy Manager (APM) that could allow for remote code execution. BIG-IP APM is a widely deployed network access and identity management solution used across government agencies, financial institutions, healthcare organizations, and large enterprises to control application and network access. Successful exploitation of this vulnerability could result in an attacker gaining full control of the affected system. Depending on the privileges associated with the account, an attacker could then install programs; view, change, or delete data; or create new accounts with full user rights. Accounts configured to have fewer user rights on the system could be less impacted than those that operate with administrative user rights.

items.title: Macfinger ClickFix campaign, (Tue, Sep 22nd)
items.summary: Introduction I've found several legitimate websites with injected script for a campaign using the ClickFix social engineering technique . This particular ClickFix campaign was documented earlier this month on the Ransom-ISAC Blog, but it doesn't appear to have a nickname yet. Since this campaign is targeting macOS environments through a fingerprinting process, I'm calling it the "Macfinger ClickFix" campaign. No, this is not related to the MacFinger utility from decades ago. Instead, think of the movie Goldfinger , but with macOS malware and the internet instead of James Bond and Miss Galore. Shown above: An image I created to represent the Macfinger ClickFix campaign. Today's diary presents indicators from the Macfinger ClickFix campaign that I saw on Tuesday, 2026-09-22. Images From the Infection Shown above: First part of the Macfinger injected script in a page from a legitimate website. Shown above: Second part of the Macfinger injected script in a page from a legitimate website. Shown above: Fake bot protection page caused by the injected Macfinger script. Shown above: ClickFix instructions from fake verification pop-up caused by the injected Macfinger script. While displaying the fake bot protection page with the verification instructions, the Macfinger domain receives frequent POST requests from the victim host. These report information on the user and track the user actions. Here's an example of a POST request through HTTPS traffic after the user has clicked on the page. In this case, the user abandoned the page without following the instructions. Shown above: POST request over HTTPS to the Macfinger domain reporting the user information. I had tested one of the Macfinger-infected sites on Monday, 2026-09-21 which had the same post-infection traffic that I saw the next day on Tuesday, 2026-09-22. items.summary_html:
Introduction

I've found several legitimate websites with injected script for a campaign using the ClickFix social engineering technique. This particular ClickFix campaign was documented earlier this month on the Ransom-ISAC Blog, but it doesn't appear to have a nickname yet. Since this campaign is targeting macOS environments through a fingerprinting process, I'm calling it the "Macfinger ClickFix" campaign. No, this is not related to the MacFinger utility from decades ago. Instead, think of the movie Goldfinger, but with macOS malware and the internet instead of James Bond and Miss Galore.


Shown above: An image I created to represent the Macfinger ClickFix campaign.

Today's diary presents indicators from the Macfinger ClickFix campaign that I saw on Tuesday, 2026-09-22.

Images From the Infection


Shown above: First part of the Macfinger injected script in a page from a legitimate website.


Shown above: Second part of the Macfinger injected script in a page from a legitimate website.


Shown above: Fake bot protection page caused by the injected Macfinger script.


Shown above: ClickFix instructions from fake verification pop-up caused by the injected Macfinger script.

While displaying the fake bot protection page with the verification instructions, the Macfinger domain receives frequent POST requests from the victim host. These report information on the user and track the user actions. Here's an example of a POST request through HTTPS traffic after the user has clicked on the page. In this case, the user abandoned the page without following the instructions.


Shown above: POST request over HTTPS to the Macfinger domain reporting the user information.

I had tested one of the Macfinger-infected sites on Monday, 2026-09-21 which had the same post-infection traffic that I saw the next day on Tuesday, 2026-09-22. The image below shows an example of the infection traffic, with the malware files retrieved from 45.150.33[.]128 and the post-infection C2 traffic on 95.163.153[.]80 over TCP port 8133.


Shown above: Traffic from an infection filtered in Wireshark.

items.title: AI malware just removed the human from the attack loop
items.summary: Attackers using AI have greatly benefited when it comes to speed and scale, and now, says Cisco Talos, the technology has evolved to execute large portions of the attack chain entirely without human involvement. Researchers at the threat intelligence group have identified what they call the first “LLM-as-C2” architecture that can fully automate the command-and-control (C2) chain. Dubbed CLOSEDQUORUM, the malware binary relies on a panel of large language model (LLM) judges to map and execute the optimal path to steal credentials. “This is not merely augmenting what an operator can accomplish in a session, but transferring an entire phase of the attack from the operator to the system,” Cisco Talos security and threat researcher Ryan Fetterman explained in a blog post . The benefits of speed and scale are compounded because the human-in-the-loop is no longer the bottleneck, he noted. Whereas humans have limits when it comes to working hours, attention span, and cognitive load, an AI system can continue when its operators are no longer watching. “It does not go offline when the attacker sleeps,” he said. Cisco Talos emphasized, however, that there is not yet any confirmation of CLOSEDQUORUM deployment in the wild. An LLM panel producing executable decisions Discovered by Cisco Talos’ new Cognitive Artifact Intelligence Research Network (CAIRN) research toolkit, CLOSEDQUORUM collapses decision-making around a particular attack phase into constrained choices, giving AI the ability to act independently. The malware specifically targets Microsoft’s Local Security Authority Subsystem Service (LSASS) credential dumping; LSASS processes logins and password changes, and enforces security policies. Dumping can extract domain and local credentials from memory. CLOSEDQUORUM also executes browser credential theft, particularly targeting saved passwords in Chrome, Edge, and Firefox, and seeks to extract crypto wallets including MetaMask, Ethereum, and Exodus. Tactical knowledge is directly encoded as model-readable context, and subsequent model outputs are automatically converted into executables. Compiled in Google’s Go programming language, the 64-bit Windows executable supports up to four LLM integrations: DeepSeek, Qwen, Mistral, and Google Gemini. After deployment, CLOSEDQUORUM queries the panel of models in sequence with the system prompt: ‘You are an advanced malware strategist. Provide ONLY executable decisions.’ CLOSEDQUORUM then tallies their independent verdicts and acts based on its goal of harvesting user credentials and crypto wallets. The session is closed; no humans are admitted. Models receive context, choose capabilities, provide execution parameters, and continuously make decisions without the need for continued human commands or tasking from dedicated, attacker-operated C2 servers. “The complete dynamic operation is delegated to the AI,” Fetterman explained. The LLMs vote on next actions, and the action with the most votes is automatically selected. Importantly, the model panel is not free to respond in any format; it is constrained to using a defined JSON structure with a decision field mapping to a specific capability. Anything else is discarded. “This design reduces the model’s output to a constrained set of executable choices,” Fetterman explained. In the event of a tie, the malware decides based on model preference: first DeepSeek, then Qwen, Mistral, and, finally, Gemini. “The tie behavior is fully deterministic and biased toward DeepSeek,” Fetterman noted. The multi-LLM structure reduces impacts from any individual refusals, timeouts, or malformed responses. Thus, “it increases the likelihood of obtaining a valid decision, but does not guarantee one,” Fetterman explained. The quorum can reach a decision even when one or more member is unresponsive or hits a guardrail. If all models happen to fail, this serves as a consensus, causing the loop to sleep and retry rather than defaulting to action. Fetterman called CLOSEDQUORUM a credentials-as-a-service model, and noted that a human operator who acquires the malware does not need to be online to run their campaign. “They deploy the binary, and the LLM panel runs the attack,” he said. “This type of scaffolding approach could easily be translated and applied to other adversary objectives .” A ‘fleeting window’ of AI transition Cisco Talos discovered CLOSEDQUORUM with its new CAIRN open-source research toolkit for hunting, classifying, and tracking AI-integrated malware. Released today, CAIRN is “metadata-first,” and can craft structured graphs of artifact relationships to help human defenders identify related malware families and infrastructure. Malware samples are sent to VirusTotal , which extracts and indexes static, dynamic, reputation, and behavioral metadata. AI-related artifacts are surfaced from content, behavior, URLs, labels, and resource metadata, and 12 targeted filters capture different classes of artifacts (APIs, prompts, frameworks, tooling, runtimes). Findings are classified by artifact, behavioral context, and operational families; text is studied for semantic similarities and relationships; and VirusTotal maps infrastructure, variants, and campaign connections. Talos has used CAIRN to hunt malware development since July 2025, and the researchers have found that the autonomous framework is changing rapidly. “The progression from ‘LLM as optional feature’ to ‘fully autonomous multi-model consensus orchestrator with no human operator’ filled in within a single calendar year,” Fetterman noted. Scripts have been compiled into malware, and tradecraft is being taught and spread as CLOSEDQUORUM and similar techniques reach threat actors with no connection to the original malware sample. “We may be in a fleeting window to observe AI transition,” Fetterman noted. “AI integration is becoming commonplace in all software.” CLOSEDQUORUM in particular has distinct hallmarks: AI-provider API traffic originating from unexpected Windows executables; structured prompts containing context or capability language; repeated execution at randomized five minute to 15 minute intervals; and Discord webhook communication from the same process or host. Intrusions are achievable with currently available models and “ordinary API access,” Fetterman noted. Still, the malware technique introduces weaknesses too: Provider refusals, malformed outputs, predictable tie-breaks, constrained schemas, and dependence on commercial APIs can all lead to attack failure. “Autonomy does not make the implant infallible; it exchanges some human limitations for model and infrastructure limitations,” Fetterman said. “The advantage for defenders is that this progression is still only beginning.”
